newsitem.title: INDIA: India four-year bond yield seen at 10.75-11.05 pct.
newsitem.headline: India four-year bond yield seen at 10.75-11.05 pct.

text.p: The latest Indian government bond issue is likely to be fully-subscribed, bank dealers and analysts polled by Reuters on Monday said, but respondents differed widely in their estimates of the cut-off yield.
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) auctions 50 billion rupees of four-year bonds later on Monday.
The poll threw up a range of 10.75 percent to 11.0 percent, with one stray estimate of 11.05. Last week, most dealers had projected a yield of 10.75-10.9 percent for the same paper.
"Conventional wisdon dictates a cut-off of around 10.75 percent," said a dealer at a European bank.
"Current secondary market yields for four-year paper are around 10.65 percent.. so add 10 basis points to make it more attractive at the auction," the dealer said.
But other dealers said the yield will be higher -- between 10.85 and 10.95 percent -- because of the issue's size.
Auctions held earlier this year have been for 20 and 30 billion rupees.
"If the RBI wants this issue to go through in full or for the market to pick up a major part, it will have to set a cut-off around 10.85-10.95 percent," said a dealer at a state-run bank.

"Given the size of the issue, I think the pattern of bidding will be slightly different this time around," the dealer said. "It will not be so easy for one or two big bidders to influence the cut-off."
At an auction of six-year bonds on July 16, the RBI set a cut-off of 11.83 percent against market expectations of 11.90-11.95 percent.
Dealers said they do not expect large bids from cash-rich provident funds or insurance companies and this will also help in a higher cut-off yield being set.
"Typically, these firms look at paper with longer tenures," said a dealer. "Most of the bids at today's auction will be from foreign or private banks and will be at higher levels."
"Further many traders have built up long positions in government securities," he said. "Prices look to be unsustainable at current levels."
